anchor.surface_text: Where a difference of treatment is based on sex, the margin of appreciation afforded to the State is narrow and in such situations the principle of proportionality does not merely require that the measure chosen should in general be suited to the fulfilment of the aim pursued, but it must also be shown that it was necessary in the circumstances.

concepts.interpretation: The Court applied the proportionality test requiring that sex-based differences in treatment must be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim.

anchor.surface_text: Article 14 of the Convention protects individuals in similar situations from being treated differently without justification in the enjoyment of their Convention rights and freedoms. This provision has no independent existence, since it has effect solely in relation to the rights and freedoms safeguarded by the other substantive provisions of the Convention and its Protocols. However, the application of Article 14 does not presuppose a breach of one or more of such provisions and to this extent it is autonomous. For Article 14 to become applicable, it suffices that the facts of a case fall within the ambit of another substantive provision of the Convention or its Protocols

concepts.interpretation: The Court explained the autonomous nature of Article 14 and its applicability when facts fall within the ambit of another substantive provision, here Article 8.

anchor.surface_text: The Court therefore considers that the applicant brought her grievances under the Convention to the attention of the appropriate judicial authorities in domestic law. Moreover, the Government have not demonstrated how an action for compensation before administrative or civil courts would provide redress for the applicant’s grievances. Nor did they provide any example in which an action for compensation before such courts had been successful in situations similar to that of the applicant. The Court accordingly rejects the Government’s objection under this head.

concepts.interpretation: The Court rejected the Government's objection for failure to exhaust remedies, noting no effective remedy was shown to exist for compensation claims in similar cases.

ITEM ID:    001-148271

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court rejected the Government's objection, noting the applicant brought her grievances to domestic courts and no effective compensation remedy was demonstrated by the Government.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that neither Article 8 nor Article 14 was applicable as the right to recruitment as a public servant is not secured by the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that neither Article 8 nor Article 14 was applicable in the instant case as it concerned a right which was not secured by the Convention, namely the right to recruitment as a public servant.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found Article 8 applicable as the applicant was appointed and subsequently dismissed, and dismissal affects private life under Article 8.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the refusal to appoint the applicant was objectively and reasonably justified due to the nature of the post reserved for male candidates.

anchor.surface_text: The Government maintained that there had been an objective and reasonable justification for the refusal of the domestic authorities to appoint the applicant to the post of security officer. They noted that the post in question had been reserved for male candidates in view of the nature of the service and the need to recruit male personnel.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no explanation or reasoning substantiating the purported inability of women to perform the post and no legitimate aim was shown.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that she had worked as a security officer and that other women had been appointed in similar cases, thus the Government's observations were irrelevant.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant submitted in reply that she had worked as a security officer in the Batman and Elazığ branches of TEDAŞ subsequent to the Ankara Administrative Court’s judgment. Besides, the administrative courts had ruled in favour of at least two other women, Y.P. and R.B., whose appointment to the posts of security officer in the Gaziantep and Batman branches of TEDAŞ had been previously refused. She considered that the Government’s observations were not relevant in the circumstances of the case.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the applicant worked in the post and other women had been appointed, undermining the Government's justification.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the length of the proceedings was not unreasonable given the case complexity and parties' conduct.

anchor.surface_text: The Government contended that the length of the proceedings could not be considered unreasonable in view of the complexity of the case and the conduct of the parties.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the length excessive and no convincing argument was provided to justify it.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the applicant had been able to submit arguments and that all decisions contained extensive reasoning, so the proceedings were fair.

anchor.surface_text: The Government maintained that the applicant had been able to submit her arguments to the domestic courts and that all decisions taken in the proceedings had contained extensive reasoning. They contended that there was nothing in the case file to show that the proceedings brought by the applicant had been unfair.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the Twelfth Division failed to consider conflicting General Assembly decision and dismissed rectification without reasoning, breaching fair hearing.

arguments.claim: The applicant maintained that the Twelfth Division failed to consider the General Assembly decision in R.B.'s case, resulting in contradictory decisions and unfair proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant maintained, in reply, that the Twelfth Division of the Supreme Administrative Court had failed to take into consideration the decision rendered by the Supreme Administrative Court’s General Assembly of Administrative Proceedings Divisions in favour of R.B. and that, as a result, the highest court had given contradictory decisions in respect of two persons in the same situation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the failure to address the conflicting decision and dismiss rectification without reasoning violated Article 6 § 1.

1.  Declares, unanimously, the application admissible;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the application was lodged within the six-month time-limit and that the applicant exhausted domestic remedies, thus admissible.

holdings.text: Holds, by six votes to one, that there has been a violation of Article 14 of the Convention, in conjunction with Article 8 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: 3.  Holds, unanimously, that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the excessive length of the proceedings;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the administrative proceedings lasted eight years with over seven years pending before the Supreme Administrative Court, which was excessive and unreasonable, breaching the reasonable time requirement under Article 6 § 1.

holdings.text: Holds, unanimously, that there has been no violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the conflicting decisions rendered by the Supreme Administrative Court

anchor.surface_text: 4 Holds, unanimously, that there has been no violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the conflicting decisions rendered by the Supreme Administrative Court;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that although conflicting decisions existed, there were no profound and long-lasting divergences and a mechanism existed to resolve inconsistencies, so no violation of Article 6 § 1 occurred.

holdings.text: Holds, unanimously, that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the absence of adequate reasoning in the Supreme Administrative Court’s decisions

anchor.surface_text: 5.  Holds, unanimously, that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the absence of adequate reasoning in the Supreme Administrative Court’s decisions;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the Twelfth Division failed to consider the conflicting General Assembly decision and dismissed rectification requests without adequate reasoning, violating the fair hearing requirement under Article 6 § 1.

holdings.text: Holds, unanimously, that the respondent State is to pay the applicant EUR 10,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage

6.  Holds, unanimously,

(a)  that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 10,000 (ten thousand euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non-pecuniary damage, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court awarded the applicant EUR 10,000 for non-pecuniary damage due to the violations found, rejecting pecuniary damage claims for lack of substantiation.
